"Corrugated" describes a surface — or an object — that has been shaped into a series of regular, parallel ridges (raised parts) and grooves (sunken channels) that alternate evenly with each other. The surface goes up, comes down, goes up, comes down, in a steady, uniform, repeating pattern — like a frozen wave, running in the same direction across the entire material.

The single most important word here is regular. Corrugated doesn't just mean "wavy" in a loose or random sense. It means the waves are deliberate, uniform, and orderly — the same height, the same depth, the same spacing, over and over, all in parallel.
How to picture it

Imagine you're looking at the sea on a very calm day, and the gentle waves are all perfectly the same height and perfectly evenly spaced. Now freeze that image solid. Flatten it into a sheet of material. That sheet — with its even, parallel ridges and valleys — is corrugated.

An even simpler way to see it: take a piece of paper and fold it back and forth like a fan. The result — a zigzag of ridges and grooves — is essentially a corrugated shape.
The most famous example: corrugated cardboard

If you've ever looked at the cut edge of a thick cardboard shipping box, you'll notice the cardboard isn't one solid block. It has two flat outer sheets, and sandwiched between them is a wavy, zigzag inner layer. That middle layer is the corrugated part. The ridges and grooves you see there are exactly what the word describes. This is probably the single most common place you encounter "corrugated" in everyday life.
Corrugated metal roofing

Think of the wavy metal sheets often used on the rooftops of sheds, warehouses, barns, and rural buildings. Those long, parallel ridges running from one end of the sheet to the other — that's corrugated iron or corrugated steel. You've almost certainly seen these if you've driven through the countryside or passed a construction site.
Corrugated roads

An unpaved dirt road, after heavy vehicle traffic, can develop a series of regular bumps and dips across its surface — from the repeated vibration of tyres pressing into the ground. This is called a corrugated road (or a washboard road). The pattern is the same: ridges and grooves, evenly spaced, running across the width of the road. Anyone who's driven on one knows the rattling, shaking feeling it produces.
Corrugated pipes and hoses

Many flexible hoses, conduits, and drainage pipes have a corrugated outer surface — you can feel the ridges running in rings around them. This design allows them to bend and flex without kinking or collapsing.
Why things are made corrugated — the deeper insight

This is what makes the word truly interesting, and understanding this will help you remember it for life.

When you take a flat, thin sheet of material — paper, metal, plastic — it is easy to bend, crush, or compress. It has almost no resistance to pressure. But when you shape that same sheet into ridges and grooves, something remarkable happens: the material becomes dramatically stronger and stiffer, without any extra material being added and without any extra weight.

The shape itself creates strength. The ridges and grooves act like tiny arches, which are one of the strongest shapes in engineering. Pressure applied to the surface has to overcome the structure of all those interlocking ridges and valleys, which distribute and resist the force far more effectively than a flat surface could.

This is why a corrugated cardboard box can protect a fragile vase during shipping — a thin flat sheet of the same cardboard couldn't. This is why corrugated metal roofs can support heavy loads of rain, snow, and their own weight. The corrugation is an engineering solution: maximum strength for minimum material.
How "corrugated" is used in sentences

To make sure you've seen the word in context: "The parcel arrived in a corrugated cardboard box." — "The old barn had a roof of corrugated iron, streaked with rust." — "After miles of corrugated road, the driver was exhausted from the constant shaking." — "The flexible drainage pipe had a corrugated surface so it could curve around corners." In every case, the image is the same: that regular, repeating pattern of ridges and grooves.
How corrugated differs from similar words

You might come across words that feel similar — here's how to keep them apart.

Corrugated vs. wavy: "Wavy" is a casual, informal word that just means something bends or curves in some wave-like way. It can be random, irregular, or loosely shaped. "Corrugated" is precise — it always means a uniform, regular, parallel pattern of ridges and grooves, usually describing an engineered or manufactured surface.

Corrugated vs. ribbed: "Ribbed" means having raised ridges or lines. But ribbed surfaces may just have raised strips — they don't necessarily have equal, matching grooves sitting between each ridge. A corrugated surface always has both: every ridge is matched by an equally sized groove right next to it, in a perfect alternation.

Corrugated vs. bumpy: "Bumpy" is informal and implies irregular, random unevenness — bumps that are different sizes and scattered without order. "Corrugated" always implies an orderly, repeating pattern.
Related word forms

The root verb is to corrugate, meaning to shape something into ridges and grooves — as in, "The machine will corrugate the steel sheet." The result of that process is something that is corrugated (the adjective you've just learned). The ridges and grooves themselves, or the overall wave-shaped structure, are called corrugations (the noun) — so you might read, "The corrugations on the roof were rusting at the edges."
In summary

"Corrugated" means shaped into a regular, repeating pattern of parallel ridges and grooves — like evenly spaced waves, all running in the same direction. The pattern always alternates: ridge, groove, ridge, groove. It is almost always the result of a deliberate manufacturing process, because the shape provides remarkable structural strength with very little extra material. When you see a wavy cardboard box, a ridged metal roof, or a flexible ribbed hose, the word for that pattern is corrugated.
